messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sovan, a 44-year-old Southeast Asian nurse, was walking to his car after a night shift when he was grabbed from behind, a knife pressed against his ribs, and his wallet and phone were taken. The attacker’s face was inches from his own, and he can still see it in perfect photographic detail—the scar above the brow, the yellowed teeth—as if the image were developed in his mind’s darkroom. Every time the memory returns, he feels a sharp, stabbing pain in his ribs exactly where the blade had been, even though there was no wound. In the weeks that followed, Sovan became convinced that something about him had made the attack happen—he had walked too slowly, or looked weak, or chosen the wrong route. This feeling of an intrinsic fault settled into a broader hopelessness: nothing good could ever come his way again, and his future had been stolen along with his phone. That same conviction—that he carried a visible flaw—kept dragging him back to the mugger’s face, as if the memory held the answer to what the attacker had seen in him.

Because he believed the attack was his own doing, Sovan began scanning every environment for clues he might have missed. At the hospital, he constantly peers around corners and checks behind supply carts before entering a room. He also catches himself looking in mirrors—the bathroom mirror, the reflective surface of the break-room microwave—searching his own face for whatever vulnerability the attacker had seen. He tells himself this vigilance will prevent another mistake, but the checking itself seems to summon the memory: the flash of silver, the grunt in his ear. The more he scans, the more the visual images intrude, and the more the pain flares in his ribs.

To keep his mind occupied, Sovan listens to podcasts constantly during his shifts and while driving. He finds that any silence invites the memory, so he fills every gap with noise. Yet the distraction fails in moments of unguarded stillness—when he wakes at 3 a.m. and stares at the ceiling, sleep shattered by a sound that was probably a car door. His sleep problems stem from a deep, wordless sense that he is never truly safe, that the mugger could be anywhere. On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay—it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome. During his commute, he constantly looks behind him, twisting his neck to scan the back seat of his own car, then the sidewalk as he walks. In the hospital cafeteria, he always chooses a seat with his back to the wall, and if that seat is taken, he leaves rather than sit exposed. The safe-seat seeking feels urgent, but it reinforces his belief that danger is pervasive and he is helpless to prevent it.

The threat he perceives also feeds back into his negative appraisals. Each time he checks behind him and feels a spike of fear, he thinks, *See? Nothing good can happen to me now.* The mugging has not only stolen the future he imagined—it has made him someone who expects pain at every turn. And the more hopeless he feels, the more he relies on his maladaptive strategies: the mirror checks, the mental noise, the constant scanning. They are his only way to manage the certainty that he is marked, that his intrinsic flaw will attract another attack.

One afternoon, while restocking supply cabinets, Sovan’s reflection startled him in the glass pane of a locked narcotics drawer. He froze, and the pain in his ribs returned so vividly that he dropped a box of syringes. A coworker asked if he was okay; he said he was fine, but later, alone in the locker room, he caught himself whispering, “I have no future.” This moment—the collision of the visual memory, the physical pain, and the hopeless appraisal—finally pushed him to seek help. He came to therapy because he is terrified that his constant vigilance is making him a worse nurse, that he will miss something real while searching for shadows. He hopes, doubtfully, that maybe there is a way to stop looking over his shoulder without being caught off guard.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals directly cause a sense of threat; instead, it shows threat causing negative appraisals, but not the reverse.
